summary: A 1970 proposal by M. Elie for a Network Interchange Language, a common way for different computers to exchange information. It is an early proposal in the series, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: If everyone spoke a different language, you would want a shared one. This proposes a common language for computers on the network.

subtitle: An early proposal for a high-level network programming language for computer networks

tldr.problem: Different computers on the ARPA network used different data formats and languages, making it difficult for them to communicate and exchange information reliably.
tldr.mechanism: NIL (Network Interchange Language) proposes a high-level language with separate sublanguages for control, operations, data declaration, and environment description, along with an abstract Network Machine concept and standard data elements called beads.
tldr.outcome: This 1970 proposal influenced thinking about network protocols and data interchange but was never formally adopted, as the networking community developed other standards like ARPANET protocols and later TCP/IP.

today: RFC 51 is a 1970 proposal from early in the ARPA network era. While NIL was never adopted as a standard, the RFC is historically significant as an early attempt to solve the problem of heterogeneous data interchange in networks. The challenge it addressed—how computers with different architectures and operating systems can reliably exchange data—was later solved through network protocols and standardized data formats like ASCII, later extensible markup languages, and structured data representations.

sections.title: The Network Interchange Language Concept
sections.content:
RFC 51, from May 1970, proposes NIL (Network Interchange Language), a high-level programming language for the ARPA network. The RFC is organized around the concept of an abstract Network Machine that presents a unified interface regardless of the underlying computer systems involved.

The core idea is that a HOST (user computer) always communicates with a Network Machine using the same language, though the Network Machine's configuration may vary depending on the remote HOST it interacts with. This abstraction aims to allow programs written in different languages on different machines to communicate as long as they can express their data structures in NIL.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine all computers on the network talked to a magical middleman who understood all languages. The middleman would translate for everyone.

sections.title: Language Sublanguages and Structure
sections.content:
NIL is divided into four sublanguages for different purposes:

  • Control sublanguage: Describes when and where computations are performed, the flow of control and ordering of operations
  • Operation sublanguage: Describes operations to be performed on data, divided into computation and data manipulation groups
  • Data declaration sublanguage: Declares variables and data structures, using standard or user-defined beads (atomic elements) as building blocks
  • Environment sublanguage: Describes the context and expected characteristics of peripherals and operating system interfaces

A complete program descriptor contains environment, data declaration, control, and operation sections. The Network Machine operates in two modes: standard mode with predefined beads and structures, and extended mode where users define custom beads and transformations.
sections.plainLanguage: The language has parts for saying what to do, how to do it, what kind of data you have, and what equipment you expect. Think of beads as Lego blocks that you snap together.

sections.title: Data Elements and Structures
sections.content:
The RFC proposes beads as the smallest indivisible units of data. Standard beads include alphanumeric types (characters, numbers), graphic types for display (MOVE, ARC), and various data structures.

Larger data structures are built from beads using VECTOR (for sequences, strings, and arrays) and PLEX (for directed graphs, trees, and rings). Control fields within structures specify linkage, modification, and parameterization. The data definition sublanguage uses a COBOL-like metalanguage for readability.
sections.plainLanguage: Beads are like atoms. You use control markers to say how they link together: in a line like a string, in a tree, in a ring.

sections.title: Implementation and Legacy
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that each HOST implement a 'generator' that accepts rules describing its data structures and environment, then generates an appropriate translator to convert data between the HOST's native format and NIL (Network Machine) format.

The document notes similarity to ALGOL and considers hardware-level translation implementations. While never formally adopted as an internet standard, RFC 51 reflects early thinking about network interchange formats and the need for a common language in heterogeneous computer networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer would have a tool that learns how that computer stores data, then translates to and from the network language. Though never built, it influenced how networks later solved this same problem.
